issues.description: In the Results, the meta-analytic effect for opportunity to connect is reported as nonsignificant (p = .065) with a 95% CI [-.01, .18] that includes zero. In the Discussion the same effect is described as 'significantly different from zero.' These statements directly contradict each other; a p of .065 with a CI spanning zero is not significant. This affects the core interpretation of one of the four key outcomes.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.subcategory: fail-safe N applied to nonsignificant result
issues.description: A fail-safe number quantifies how many null studies would be needed to reduce a significant result to nonsignificance. The connect meta-analytic effect was already nonsignificant (p = .065), so a positive FSN (5) is conceptually inapplicable/uninterpretable and should be zero. Reporting an FSN here reflects a misuse of the method.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065. A forest plot is presented in Figure 2. The replication between-study variance showed limited evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 10.79, p = .095; T2 = .006, 95% CI [0, .09]; I2 = 44.39%, 95% CI [0%, 91.69%]. The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.description: FSN values for the same outcomes differ between Results and Discussion. For Express, Results report FSN = 3 but Discussion states 'only five unreported studies.' For Connect, Results report FSN = 5 but Discussion states 'low FSN (11 studies).' These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported analyses and the robustness conclusions drawn from them.
issues.quote: These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent original effect size for advantages
issues.description: The original study's advantageous self-disclosure effect is reported as -.30 in the Abstract and Table 1 (β = -.300), but as -.33 in Table 3 and in the Discussion ('-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33'). The reader cannot determine which value was actually used in the effect-size-difference computations, affecting all advantage comparisons.
issues.quote: Self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)

issues.description: In the Discussion the safety prediction interval is reported as [-.40, -.15], but Results report the 95% CI as [-.40, -.15] and the 95% PI as [-.54, -.03]. The Discussion mislabels the confidence interval as a prediction interval, which materially changes the inference about the range of expected future effects.
issues.quote: The 95% PI [-.40, -.15] indicated that future studies would be likely to find such an effect as well.

issues.description: The connect prediction interval is reported as [-.09, .26] in Results but as [-.07, .27] in the Discussion. These discrepant intervals indicate either transcription errors or differing analyses, and both are used to support interpretive claims.
issues.quote: supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero

issues.description: The authors repeatedly attribute the larger original effect sizes to 'publication bias in the original study.' Publication bias is a property of a body of literature, not a single study, and cannot be inferred from one original study having a larger effect than replications (which could equally reflect sampling error, declining effects, contextual change, or regression to the mean). This is an inappropriate causal/inferential claim.
issues.quote: the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study’s, all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study

issues.description: For expression, the meta-analytic effect was r = .08, p = .021, statistically different from zero, yet the authors interpret this as confirming 'the same lack of an effect.' Treating a significant pooled effect as a null finding is internally contradictory and reflects selective emphasis on the individual-study CIs over the pooled estimate.
issues.quote: led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications

issues.subcategory: beta equated with r across models
issues.description: The authors assert 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient,' which holds only for simple bivariate regression with a single predictor. They also state self-esteem was mean-centered (typically done when interactions/covariates are present). If the original or replication models included additional predictors, standardized beta would not equal r, biasing the effect-size extraction and all comparisons. The model specification is not clearly reported.
issues.quote: Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: selection of studies within CREP forks
issues.description: Seventeen teams began the replication ('17 forks') but only seven met the minimum sample size and posted data/results. The fate and characteristics of the other ten are not described. Excluding teams that failed to reach N or did not post results could introduce selection bias into the meta-analysis (a within-project file-drawer), which is not analyzed or acknowledged.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 “forks” representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process (see https://osf.io/pcmq5/forks/). These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository.

issues.description: The authors acknowledge that missing-data procedures, composite-score calculation, and exclusions are unknown for several studies, and that one site (Gordon) appears to have summed rather than averaged items. Inconsistent and undocumented data handling across primary studies compromises the comparability of effect sizes entering the meta-analysis and limits replicability.
issues.quote: Contributors did not always post analysis scripts, so procedures to account for missing data are not known for all studies. Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale was administered with a 4-point scale in most studies but a 5-point scale in two, and one study altered item wording and order. Combining measures with differing response formats and wording into a single meta-analysis introduces measurement heterogeneity that is not modeled (and the small number of studies precludes moderation analysis).
issues.quote: (a) one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., ‘At times I think I am no good at all’ vs. ‘I think I am no good at all’), and (b) most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.subcategory: underpowered minimum sample / uncontrolled procedural variation
issues.description: Minimum N was set at 80 (the original's size), which is underpowered for detecting small effects and especially for the effect-size-difference comparisons the authors emphasize (Goal 5). Additionally, procedural variations (lab vs. online, individual vs. group administration of 2–6, added measures) were confounded with site and could not be tested as moderators given only seven studies. While partly acknowledged, this limits the strength of any inference.
issues.quote: collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (80 for the present study as this was the sample size in the original study)

issues.description: All replication samples were US undergraduates from five institutions, yet the abstract claims the results speak to the original study's 'generalizability and robustness.' The homogeneous student samples (and the platform-specific, time-bound nature of Facebook use) limit generalization, and the claim is stronger than the data support.
issues.quote: The results provided further evidence regarding the original study’s generalizability and robustness.

issues.description: The authors discount the original connect finding by arguing that p-values between .04 and .05 are more likely under the null. This argument is invoked selectively (only for the result that failed to replicate) and is used to bolster a preferred conclusion, reflecting interpretive flexibility rather than a principled, pre-specified criterion.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that the original study obtained a p-value of .05, and p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one (Lakens & Evers, 2014; Masicampo & Lelande, 2012).

issues.description: The dependent measures assess perceived safety/advantages of self-disclosure, not actual disclosure behavior. The Discussion at points slips into claims about the 'tendency to self-disclose' and behavioral compensation, conflating perceptions with behavior—a mismatch between the operationalized construct and the conclusions drawn.
issues.quote: Self-disclosures on Facebook can be made without some of the immediate indicators of disapproval present in FTF interactions, and thus increase the tendency to self-disclose (Hollenbaugh & Ferris, 2014).

issues.subcategory: interpretation of fail-safe N as evidence for a null
issues.description: The authors interpret the FSN to argue that future replications would confirm a 'lack of an effect.' FSN addresses how many additional null studies would overturn a significant effect; it does not provide evidence for the absence of an effect, and a small FSN (3) actually indicates fragility, not confidence. This is a misinterpretation of the statistic.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: missing original model details and express effect derivation
issues.description: The original study did not report a beta for expression (Table 1 shows 'n/a'), yet an original effect size r = .15 is used in Table 3 and the meta-analytic comparisons. The method of deriving this value (e.g., from a t-statistic) and the exact model specification of the original regressions are not adequately reported, hindering evaluation and replication of the effect-size extraction.
issues.quote: The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.

issues.description: The safety outcome showed substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 71.76%, Q p = .005), yet a single pooled estimate is emphasized and described as 'considerable' and robust (FSN 133). With high heterogeneity and only seven studies (and acknowledged bias in small-k heterogeneity estimates), strong summary claims about a single 'considerable' effect size are not well justified.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions, and that the size of this effect is considerable.

issues.description: Although the project is described as preregistered with open data, analysis scripts were not consistently posted, scoring differed across sites, and the meta-analytic decisions (REML, random effects, FSN, effect-size-difference method) were chosen by the meta-analysts rather than preregistered for the synthesis. This combination of undocumented primary-study analyses and post hoc synthesis choices introduces researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Another impediment to drawing better conclusions relate to some of the variations in the studies. For example, not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.
